questions.prompt: For an ideal op-amp, the inverting amplifier in the figure has closed-loop gain \(v_{out}/v_{in}\) equal to
questions.explanation:
With the \(+\) input grounded, the inverting input is a virtual ground. The input current \(v_{in}/R_1\) must flow through \(R_2\) (the op-amp draws none), so \(v_{out}=0-\dfrac{v_{in}}{R_1}R_2\Rightarrow\dfrac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=-\dfrac{R_2}{R_1}\) (reader Eq. 17.41).
• \(1+R_2/R_1\) is the NON-inverting gain.
• \(R_1/R_2\) flips the ratio; the feedback resistor goes in the numerator.

questions.prompt: In an inverting amplifier with an ideal op-amp and a normal output (not saturated), the inverting-input voltage \(V^-\) is very close to 0 V. Why?
options: Because the inverting input is physically connected to ground
The huge gain forces \(V^+-V^-\) to be tiny, and \(V^+\) is grounded, so \(V^-\approx0\) (a virtual ground)
Because the op-amp draws a large current from the input
questions.explanation:
\(v_{out}=A(V^+-V^-)\) with finite \(v_{out}\) and \(A\to\infty\) requires \(V^+-V^-\to0\). Since \(V^+=0\), \(V^-\approx0\): a 'virtual' ground, at 0 V but NOT connected to ground.
• The node isn't wired to ground; it sits at 0 V because of feedback.
• Any resistor values give a virtual ground.
• The input current of an ideal op-amp is zero.

questions.prompt: The inverting amplifier has \(R_1=2\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\), \(R_2=10\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) and \(v_{in}=0.3\ \mathrm{V}\). With an ideal op-amp, what is \(v_{out}\)?
questions.explanation:
Gain \(=-R_2/R_1=-10/2=-5\), so \(v_{out}=-5\times0.3\ \mathrm{V}=-1.5\ \mathrm{V}\).
Check with currents: \(i=0.3/2\ \mathrm{k\Omega}=150\ \mu\mathrm{A}\) flows through \(R_2\), dropping \(150\ \mu\mathrm{A}\times10\ \mathrm{k\Omega}=1.5\ \mathrm{V}\) from the virtual ground (0 V) down to \(v_{out}=-1.5\ \mathrm{V}\).

questions.prompt: An inverting amplifier uses \(R_1=4.7\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) and \(R_2=47\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) (ideal op-amp). What resistance does the source \(v_{in}\) see looking into the input terminal?
questions.explanation:
The right end of \(R_1\) is the virtual ground, so \(i_{in}=\dfrac{v_{in}-0}{R_1}\) and \(R_{in}=\dfrac{v_{in}}{i_{in}}=R_1=4.7\ \mathrm{k\Omega}=4700\ \Omega\).
Unlike the non-inverting amplifier (\(R_{in}\to\infty\)), the inverting amplifier loads its source with exactly \(R_1\), a design constraint when the source is weak. Common mistake: answering \(R_1+R_2\) or \(R_1\parallel R_2\).

questions.prompt: The amplifier has \(R_1=1\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\), \(R_2=9\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) (ideal gain \(-9\)), but the op-amp has finite gain \(A=1000\). The exact gain is \(\dfrac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=\dfrac{-A\,g}{1+A\,f}\) with \(g=\dfrac{R_2}{R_1+R_2}\), \(f=\dfrac{R_1}{R_1+R_2}\). What is it?
questions.explanation:
\(f=0.1\), \(g=0.9\). Then \(\dfrac{-1000(0.9)}{1+1000(0.1)}=\dfrac{-900}{101}=-8.911\).
That is 1% smaller in magnitude than the ideal \(-9\): the loop gain \(T=Af=100\), so the error is about \(1/(1+T)\) (reader Eq. 17.40). Common mistake: using \(A\,f\) in place of \(A\,g\) in the numerator.

questions.prompt: In the inverting amplifier with an ideal op-amp, \(R_2\) is doubled while \(R_1\) and \(v_{in}\) stay fixed. What happens to the current through \(R_1\)?
options: It is unchanged: the virtual ground holds the right end of \(R_1\) at 0 V regardless of \(R_2\)
questions.explanation:
\(i_1=\dfrac{v_{in}-V^-}{R_1}=\dfrac{v_{in}}{R_1}\) because \(V^-\approx0\). Doubling \(R_2\) changes the OUTPUT voltage (the same current through a larger resistor, \(v_{out}=-i_1R_2\)), not the input current. This independence is why one can trim the gain with \(R_2\) without disturbing the source.
• The current would only change if the virtual-ground assumption broke (for example the output saturated).

questions.prompt: Which closed-loop voltage gain can be realized with a single ideal-op-amp stage (inverting or non-inverting)?
questions.explanation:
The inverting gain \(-R_2/R_1\) can have any magnitude, including less than 1, but is always negative. The non-inverting gain \(1+R_2/R_1\) is always \(\ge 1\) (with \(R_2=0\) it is a follower). So the correct choice is \(-0.1\); a positive gain below 1 needs an extra divider.
• \(+0.5\) and \(0\) are impossible for non-inverting (\(\ge1\)).
• An inverting stage always gives a NEGATIVE gain, so \(+0.9\) is impossible.

questions.prompt: Supplies are \(\pm12\ \mathrm{V}\), \(R_2/R_1=20\) and \(v_{in}=0.8\ \mathrm{V}\) (otherwise ideal op-amp). What is \(v_{out}\)?
options: About \(-12\ \mathrm{V}\) (clipped at the negative rail; the ideal result of \(-16\ \mathrm{V}\) is impossible)
\(0\ \mathrm{V}\), since the virtual ground forces zero output
questions.explanation:
The ideal equation gives \(-20\times0.8=-16\ \mathrm{V}\), beyond the supply. The output cannot exceed the rails (reader Sec. 18.4.1), so it clips at about \(-12\ \mathrm{V}\) (in practice a bit less).
While clipped, the feedback loop is no longer in control: the input terminals are no longer at the same voltage, so the 'virtual ground' assumption (and the gain formula) fails. The largest linear input is \(12/20=0.6\ \mathrm{V}\).
• The virtual ground is at the inverting INPUT, not the output.

questions.prompt: An op-amp has a gain-bandwidth product (unity-gain frequency) of 1 MHz. Used as an inverting amplifier with \(R_1=1\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\), \(R_2=9\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\), what is the closed-loop gain-bandwidth product \(|A_{cl}|\cdot BW\), in kHz? (Reader Eq. 17.43: \(GBW=A_0\,g\,\omega_{-3dB}\).)
questions.explanation:
The closed-loop bandwidth is \(\dfrac{f_u}{1+R_2/R_1}=\dfrac{1\ \mathrm{MHz}}{10}=100\ \mathrm{kHz}\) (set by \(f\), as for the non-inverting amplifier). But the DC gain magnitude is only \(R_2/R_1=9\), not 10, because the input is attenuated by \(g=0.9\).
Product: \(9\times100\ \mathrm{kHz}=900\ \mathrm{kHz}=g\,f_u\), 10% below the non-inverting amplifier's \(1\ \mathrm{MHz}\). Common mistake: assuming GBW is always the op-amp's 1 MHz.
Reader typo: Eq. 17.42 writes \(v_o/v_o\); it should be \(v_o/v_s\).

questions.prompt: Preview of common-source gain (an inverting stage in disguise). Two sources feed the inverting node through \(10\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) and \(20\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) resistors, with \(R_2=40\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) feedback (ideal op-amp). With \(v_1=0.2\ \mathrm{V}\) and \(v_2=-0.1\ \mathrm{V}\), what is \(v_{out}\)?
questions.explanation:
The inverting node is a virtual ground, so the input currents add: \(i=\dfrac{v_1}{10\ \mathrm{k}}+\dfrac{v_2}{20\ \mathrm{k}}=20\ \mu\mathrm{A}-5\ \mu\mathrm{A}=15\ \mu\mathrm{A}\).
All of it flows through \(R_2\): \(v_{out}=-iR_2=-15\ \mu\mathrm{A}\times40\ \mathrm{k\Omega}=-0.6\ \mathrm{V}\), i.e. \(-(4v_1+2v_2)\) (a weighted sum). Later you will meet transistor amplifiers whose gain is also an inverting ratio \(-g_mR\); the same virtual-ground thinking helps.

questions.prompt: Preview of transimpedance. A photodiode is modeled as a \(2\ \mu\mathrm{A}\) current source driving the inverting input of an ideal-op-amp inverting stage with \(R_2=500\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) (no \(R_1\)). The current flows into the inverting node. What is \(v_{out}\)?
questions.explanation:
The virtual ground absorbs the source current with no voltage developed at the input, and the op-amp pushes that entire current through \(R_2\) (the op-amp draws none): \(v_{out}=0-i\,R_2=-2\ \mu\mathrm{A}\times500\ \mathrm{k\Omega}=-1.0\ \mathrm{V}\).
The circuit converts current to voltage with gain \(-R_2\) (a 'transimpedance' amplifier, as the reader notes the inverting amplifier really is). The virtual ground keeps the source operating at 0 V, which matters for photodiodes and other current-output sensors.

questions.prompt: Preview of the Miller effect and integrators. In the inverting stage the feedback resistor is replaced by a capacitor \(C=100\ \mathrm{nF}\), with \(R=10\ \mathrm{k\Omega}\) at the input. A \(1\ \mathrm{V}\) step is applied at \(t=0\) (initial output 0 V, ideal op-amp). How fast does \(v_{out}\) change?
questions.explanation:
The virtual ground gives a constant input current \(i=\dfrac{1\ \mathrm{V}}{10\ \mathrm{k\Omega}}=100\ \mu\mathrm{A}\), and that same current charges \(C\): \(i=-C\dfrac{dv_{out}}{dt}\).
So \(\dfrac{dv_{out}}{dt}=-\dfrac{i}{C}=-\dfrac{100\ \mu\mathrm{A}}{100\ \mathrm{nF}}=-10^{3}\ \mathrm{V/s}=-1\ \mathrm{V/ms}\).
The inverting sign (the output goes negative for a positive input) and the ramp are the point: a capacitor in the feedback path of an inverting amplifier will later appear as an enlarged input capacitance (Miller effect).
